Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones
Medical equipment such as needles or drips

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I try to push them out of my mind

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: I acted in ways that go against who I am
I have permanently changed for the worse
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Weapons): Weapons or objects used as weapons
issues.explanation: For trauma type of a child's life-threatening illness, weapon-related visual triggers are hard to reconcile unless there is additional unreported violent trauma. Hospital smells and loss-related conversations fit, but weapons/object-as-weapon cues are clinically implausible for the same index trauma.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'You can never know who will harm you' implies interpersonal danger/assailant threat, which is poorly matched to the validated trauma of a child's serious illness. This also aligns awkwardly with the rest of the profile, which is otherwise illness/loss/moral injury themed rather than assault-based.

issues.item: Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
issues.explanation: 'Intense rage on recall' is hard to reconcile with the rest of this profile for an 80-year-old mother traumatized by a child's life-threatening illness. The other items center on helplessness, permanent change, loss-related and hospital triggers, and intrusive affect without image. Distress, fear, guilt, grief, or sadness would fit more coherently; rage is not impossible, but here it is insufficiently supported by any corresponding appraisal or trigger content and stands out as clinically incongruent.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Face Hiding: cover face with hands
issues.explanation: 'Cover face with hands' is not well supported as a maladaptive strategy in this profile. The active formulation links maladaptive strategies mainly to negative appraisals and memory, and the other strategies chosen (avoid going out, thought suppression) fit intrusive distress and negative beliefs. Face hiding is more typical of acute shame/panic/social exposure and is not clearly connected to the hospital/loss triggers, intrusive memory pattern, or appraisals provided, making it the least coherent item in this set.

vignette: The summer Amira’s twenty-three-year-old son, Tariq, collapsed from septic shock, the world narrowed to the sterile, antiseptic air of the intensive care unit and the relentless rhythm of dialysis pumps. She watched nurses adjust IV drips and overheard physicians quietly discuss prognosis with families already preparing for loss. That night became the anchor of her trauma. When the sharp, chemical scent of a hospital corridor or the glint of a syringe surfaced in her daily life, it did not merely recall the past; the uncontrolled access of her trauma memory would seize her, dumping the full, unfiltered emotional intensity of that ICU night without any clear image. The visceral force of these sudden surges immediately convinced her that she had permanently altered for the worse, that her professional identity as a compassionate social worker had been stripped away by profound helplessness. That conviction, paired with the belief that she simply could not stop bad things from happening to those she cared about, dictated her daily choices. She stopped going out to neighborhood gatherings, strictly avoided medical cues like ambulance sirens and physical examinations, and relied on thought suppression, forcing herself to push the recollections out of her mind during work hours. As the following months unfolded, this pattern calcified into a quiet but inescapable feedback loop. Her conviction of permanent damage and helplessness acted as a cognitive lens that warped how her memories surfaced. Instead of fading with time, the recollections were systematically amplified by her belief that the trauma had permanently altered her, making the sudden, imageless emotional surges feel even more invasive and inescapable. Simultaneously, those negative appraisals sharpened her attention to loss themes. She found herself scanning every group discussion or client intake for whispers about bereavement, her heightened vigilance ensuring that ordinary conversations about grief suddenly felt dangerously amplified. When she fixated on those loss themes, they did not remain abstract; they triggered the next wave of uncontrolled, imageless recall, leaving her breathless and disoriented in the middle of a home visit. The cycle tightened further when her avoidance strategies quietly confirmed her worst fears. By retreating from medical settings and suppressing her thoughts, she systematically eliminated the very opportunities to disprove her helplessness, leaving the belief that she was fundamentally changed for the worse to remain unchallenged and absolute. She continued to work as a social worker, but her daily environment became a carefully controlled space. She relocated her caseload to a quiet community outreach office, deliberately routing her walks away from clinic entrances, and she still flinched when a visiting nurse approached a senior client with a vein finder and needles. During routine wellness checks, the mere sight of medical equipment would trigger a spike of panic, forcing her to excuse herself and retreat to her car. These clinical encounters reinforced her core beliefs: every time she witnessed a patient’s deterioration, her negative appraisals flared, convincing her that her own helplessness was contagious and that she had permanently damaged her capacity to protect anyone. To survive the emotional weight, she relied on thought suppression, mentally rehearsing case notes to drown out the grief on recall. Yet this very suppression only deepened her conviction that she was fundamentally changed for the worse, because avoiding the feelings prevented her from processing them, ensuring that the negative appraisals remained intact. Now at eighty, Amira seeks therapy not because the symptoms have intensified, but because the exhaustion of maintaining this quiet vigilance is fracturing her remaining relationships and her professional identity. She is most afraid that her avoidance has quietly isolated her from the community she spent a lifetime serving, and what she hopes for is simply to reclaim the ability to move through her days without bracing for another collapse that never comes.
